clues.text: I played a role in helping bring some of the Ten Plagues upon Egypt.
I made a golden calf for the Israelites.
I served as Israel's first high priest.
I spoke to Pharaoh on behalf of Moses.
I was Moses' brother.
My sister was Miriam.
God made me Moses' spokesman because I could speak very well.
My rod swallowed the rods of Egypt's magic-practicing priests.
I entered the priesthood together with four sons.
My sons included Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
I met Moses in the wilderness after Jehovah sent me to him.
I was eighty-three years old when I spoke to Pharaoh.
I was instructed to wear a breastpiece bearing the names of Israel's tribes.
God said I would serve as a prophet to Moses.
Fire came out from Jehovah and consumed the offering I made on behalf of the people.
I built an altar before a calf and called for a festival to Jehovah.
I held up one of Moses' hands during a battle, while Hur held the other.
I pleaded with Moses after Miriam was struck with leprosy.
I tried to explain how a calf appeared, saying that it came out after gold was thrown into a fire.
I went up a mountain with Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders of Israel.
I wore the Urim and the Thummim over my heart when going in before Jehovah.
Incense in my hand helped stop a plague among the Israelites.
My rod budded, blossomed, and produced ripe almonds.
Together with Miriam, I spoke against Moses because of his wife.
I wore the breastpiece of judgement.
I married Elisheba, Amminadab's daughter.
I died on Mount Hor.
I stood between the dead and the living while a plague was halted.
I was forbidden from entering the Promised Land because of an incident involving water from a crag.
I was older than Moses by three years.
After two of my sons died for offering unauthorized fire, I kept silent.
Jehovah told me to bless Israel with the words, “May Jehovah bless you and safeguard you.”
Korah and his company gathered together against Moses and me.
My priestly garments were removed and given to my son before I died.
My rod was kept before the Testimony as a sign to the rebels.
The entire house of Israel mourned me for thirty days.
One of my brothers was named Dathan.
I came out and took my stand at the entrance of my tent with Dathan and our families.
I rose up against Moses with Korah.
I accused Moses of failing to give the Israelites an inheritance of field and vineyard.
I said Moses had brought the people up only to put them to death in the wilderness.
I was a Reubenite son of Eliab.
I was one of the chosen ones of the assembly who fought against Moses and Aaron.
When Moses sent for me, I said I was not going to come.
One of my brothers was named Nemuel.
I stood at my tent entrance with my wife, my sons, and my little children while the assembly of Israel moved away from us.
Moses said that if the ground opened and swallowed me alive, Israel would know I had treated Jehovah disrespectfully.
Moses told the assembly not to touch anything that belonged to me, my brother or our families.
My tents and household were swallowed before the eyes of all Israel.
A psalmist said that the earth covered those assembled with me.
I went down alive into the Grave with all who belonged to me.
Moses mentioned what God did to me as a reminder, before Israel entered the promised land.
My judgment proved that my opposition was against Jehovah, not only against Moses.
The earth opened and swallowed me, and I became a warning example.
I secretly kept some of the spoils from Jericho.
I took things that had been devoted to destruction.
My theft brought trouble on all Israel.
A military defeat helped expose what I had done in secret.
I belonged to the tribe of Judah.
I took a beautiful garment from Shinar, silver, and a bar of gold.
Joshua spoke directly to me before I confessed my wrongdoing.
The items I stole were found buried beneath my tent.
A sacred lot was used to identify me.
I admitted that I saw, desired, and took forbidden items.
I said, "I am the one who sinned against Jehovah the God of Israel."
Israel burned me with fire after stoning me.
My household was examined before I was singled out.
The place where I was judged was called the Valley of Achor.
A pile of stones was raised after judgment was executed on me.
All Israel stoned me in a valley.
I was the son of Carmi.
My desire for forbidden items played a role in my downfall.
Silver weighing 200 shekels and a gold bar weighing 50 shekels became evidence against me.
The defeat at Ai was linked to what I had done.
My donkey spoke to me.
I was hired to curse Israel.
An angel stood in my path with a drawn sword.
I blessed Israel when others wanted me to curse them.
I said only what Jehovah allowed me to say.
Messengers carrying divination fees came to me.
I lived near the Euphrates River.
I asked God for direction after receiving visitors from Moab.
I rose early in the morning and sent visiting officials away.
I said, "Even if Balak should give me his house full of silver and gold, I could not go beyond the order of Jehovah my God."
I saddled my donkey and traveled with Moabite officials.
My donkey saw danger that I could not see.
I struck my donkey three times.
I bowed low after my eyes were uncovered.
I offered sacrifices from three different locations overlooking Israel.
I declared, "How can I curse whom God has not cursed?"
I foretold that a star would come out of Jacob.
The spirit of God came upon me while I was delivering a prophecy.
I said, "Let me die the death of the upright."
I described myself as a man whose eye had been opened.
I compared Israel's tents to valleys, gardens, and aloes planted by Jehovah.
I was present when a king struck his hands together in anger.
My counsel later became associated with Israel's sin involving Moab and Peor.
I was killed by the sword during Israel's campaign against Midian.
Centuries later, my name was used as a warning against greed and corrupt influence.
I offered rewards in an attempt to influence a prophet.
I sent for Balaam because I wanted Israel to be cursed.
I was a king of Moab.
I was afraid because the Israelites had become very numerous.
I believed a curse could help me defeat a nation.
I honored a visitor whom I hoped would curse Israel.
I said, "Come, now, do curse this people for me."
I sent a second group of officials after my first request was unsuccessful.
I sent messengers to a man living near the Euphrates River.
I became angry when blessings were pronounced instead of curses.
I built altars and provided sacrifices in an effort to obtain a curse.
I moved from one location to another hoping for a different prophecy.
I struck my hands together in frustration.
I took someone to view part of Israel's camp before asking for a curse.
A prophecy about a star coming out of Jacob was delivered while I was present.
I took a prophet to Bamoth-baal, the field of Zophim, and the top of Peor.
I was told, "How can I curse whom God has not cursed?"
Jehovah later reminded Israel of the counsel I gave and of Balaam's answer.
Joshua later recalled that I fought against Israel and that I hired Balaam to curse them.
My attempts to curse Israel resulted in repeated blessings instead.
Jehovah chose me to help build the tabernacle.
I was filled with God's spirit for craftsmanship.
I worked on the construction of the tabernacle and its furnishings.
Oholiab worked alongside me.
I was given wisdom, understanding, and knowledge for a special assignment.
I was skilled in working with gold, silver, and copper.
I was skilled in stonecutting and wood carving.
Jehovah specifically called me by name.
I helped teach others the skills needed for sacred construction work.
I received contributions from the Israelites for a major building project.
The people kept bringing me more materials than were needed.
I helped create the Ark of the Covenant.
I made two gold cherubs whose wings overshadowed a sacred cover.
I made the table used for the showbread.
I made the lampstand from pure gold.
I made the incense altar.
I made the altar for burnt offerings.
I made the copper basin and its stand.
My grandfather was Hur.
I was the son of Uri.
The record says that I did everything just as Jehovah had commanded Moses.
Along with Job's other two companions, I did not recognize him from a distance and began to weep loudly.
Along with Job's other two companions, I did what Jehovah required, and Job prayed for me.
Along with Job's other two companions, I sat with him on the ground for seven days and seven nights in silence.
I answered Job more than once during his suffering.
I came from my own place with Job's other two companions to comfort him.
Jehovah's anger burned against Job's three companions, including me, for what had been said about Him.
Along with Job's other two companions, I offered seven bulls and seven rams as Jehovah required.
I asked whether God would pervert justice, or the Almighty pervert righteousness.
I met by agreement with Eliphaz and Zophar before going to Job.
I said God will not reject those who keep integrity, nor support evil men.
I said that if Job's sons had sinned against God, He let them be punished for their revolt.
I said that those living only a short while know nothing, for their days on earth are a shadow.
I told Job that if he were truly pure and upright, God would restore him to his rightful place.
I urged Job to ask the former generation and pay attention to what their fathers found out.
I was a Shuhite.
After my shortest speech of all, I stopped answering Job along with his other two companions.
I asked whether a papyrus plant can grow tall where there is no marsh.
I asked why Job's companions should be viewed as animals and considered stupid in his eyes.
I compared mortal man to a maggot, and a son of man to a worm.
I compared the hope of the godless to something as fragile as a spider's web.
I described the wicked man's feet leading him into a net, with snares catching his heel.
I said even the moon is not bright and the stars are not pure in God's eyes.
I said sulfur would be scattered on the wicked man's home.
I said the light of the wicked will be extinguished, and the lamp over him will go out.
I said the wicked man is torn from his tent and marched to the king of terrors.
I asked how mortal man can be righteous before God, or how one born of a woman can be innocent.
I pictured the wicked with no offspring among his people.
I said the memory of the wicked would fade from the earth, and in the street his name would be unknown.
I told Job that though his beginning was small, his future would be great if he looked to God.
I said that rulership and fearsome power belong to God, who establishes peace in the heights.
I represented the tribe of Judah among the twelve spies sent into Canaan.
Joshua and I encouraged Israel to enter the Promised Land.
I survived the wilderness journey while most of my generation did not.
I received Hebron as an inheritance.
I followed Jehovah wholeheartedly.
I tried to calm the people after the spies gave their report.
I said, "Let us go up immediately, and we will certainly conquer it."
I saw giants in the land but still believed we could take it.
I was the son of Jephunneh.
I tore my garments when the people talked about rebelling.
I said that the inhabitants of Canaan would be bread for us.
I was nearly stoned for encouraging faith in Jehovah's promise.
Jehovah said that I had a different spirit from the rest of the people.
I crossed the Jordan after spending about forty years in the wilderness.
I said that I was still as strong as I had been decades earlier.
At eighty-five years of age, I asked for a mountainous region as my inheritance.
I requested the very area where the Anakim lived.
I drove out Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai.
I said, "Give me this mountainous region."
My daughter Achsah asked me for springs of water.
I offered my daughter in marriage to the man who captured Kiriath-sepher.
Othniel became my son-in-law.
My inheritance remained with my descendants because I followed Jehovah wholeheartedly.
I rebelled against Moses with Korah.
I was from the tribe of Reuben.
The earth opened and swallowed me.
I accused Moses of wanting to make himself an absolute ruler.
Abiram and I accused Moses of bringing us up out of a land flowing with milk and honey.
I refused to come when Moses sent for me.
I was a chosen one of the assembly who fought against Moses and Aaron.
I was a son of Eliab.
I also had a brother named Nemuel.
I asked Moses whether he would bore out the eyes of those men.
I belonged to the line of Pallu through my father Eliab.
I said Moses had not brought Israel into any land flowing with milk and honey.
I said Moses had not given an inheritance of field and vineyard.
I took my stand at the entrance of my tent with my wife, my sons, and my little children.
Moses came to me with the elders of Israel.
The assembly was told to get away from around my tent before I was judged.
After the earth swallowed me, I became a warning example.
An inspired song recalled that the earth opened up and swallowed me.
I fought against Moses and Aaron along with Korah's group, and against Jehovah.
I went down alive into the Grave, and the earth covered me over.
Moses later reminded Israel of what Jehovah did to me and my brother before all Israel's eyes.
My household, my tents, and every living thing that followed me were swallowed with me.
I became high priest after my father died.
My father was Aaron.
Joshua and I helped divide the Promised Land among the tribes.
I survived when two of my brothers offered unauthorized fire.
My brothers Nadab and Abihu died before Jehovah.
My father removed his priestly garments and placed them on me before he died.
I was from the tribe of Levi.
I supervised the oil of the lighting, incense, grain offering, and anointing oil used at the tabernacle.
I married one of the daughters of Putiel.
My son was Phinehas.
I was instructed to consult the Urim when guidance was needed for Joshua.
I helped count the Israelites on the plains of Moab.
I participated in the distribution of conquered Midianite spoil.
My son was sent with representatives of the tribes to investigate an altar built near the Jordan.
My son approved the explanation given by the tribes east of the Jordan regarding a disputed altar.
I came down from Mount Hor with Moses after receiving my father's priestly garments following his death there.
I died and was buried at Gibeah, a city associated with my son.
When David divided the priesthood, more headmen were found among my sons than among Ithamar's sons.
I spoke after Job's three companions stopped answering him.
I became angry with Job and his three companions.
I was younger than the men I addressed.
I waited before speaking because I respected the age of those present.
I said, "Days themselves should speak, And a multitude of years should make wisdom known."
I believed that age alone does not guarantee wisdom.
I listened carefully while older men searched for answers to Job's arguments.
I said that I was full of words and compelled to speak.
I compared myself to wineskins ready to burst.
I promised not to show partiality or flatter anyone.
I said that God speaks in more than one way even when people do not notice it.
I described dreams and visions as one way God may communicate.
I said that God is greater than mortal man.
I urged Job to listen while I continued speaking.
I declared that true justice cannot be perverted by God.
I argued that God repays a person according to his actions.
I spoke about the formation of ice, snow, rain, and clouds.
I described thunder as the voice of God.
I was the son of Barachel the Buzite.
I was from the family of Ram.
I finished speaking immediately before Jehovah answered out of the windstorm.
After Jehovah spoke to me, Job prayed for his three companions, including me.
Along with Job's other two companions, I did not recognize him from a distance.
Along with Job's other two companions, I sat on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights without saying a word.
I argued with Job about why he was suffering.
I came with Job's other two companions to sympathize with him and comfort him.
Jehovah told me that my two companions and I had not spoken the truth about Him as Job had.
Along with Job's other two companions, I ripped my garments apart and threw dust onto my head.
Along with Job's other two companions, I took seven bulls and seven rams and offered up a burnt sacrifice.
I agreed with Bildad and Zophar to meet together before going to Job.
I asked what innocent person had ever perished, or when the upright had been destroyed.
I reminded Job that he had once strengthened weak hands and buckling knees.
I said man is born for trouble as surely as sparks fly upward.
I said those who plow what is harmful and sow trouble will reap the same.
I said, “Happy is the man whom God reproves.”
I spoke first among Job's three companions.
I urged Job not to reject the discipline of the Almighty.
I was a Temanite.
Jehovah addressed me when He rebuked Job's companions.
I told Job that a word was brought to me in secret, and a whisper of it reached my ear.
Along with Job's other two companions, I stopped answering him when he remained convinced of his own righteousness.
During a night vision, a spirit passed over my face and the hair of my flesh bristled.
I accused Job of holding back food from the hungry and sending widows away empty-handed.
I accused Job of seizing a pledge from his brothers for no reason.
I asked if Job had been the first man ever born, or if his birth was before that of the hills.
I compared mortal men to those dwelling in houses of clay, crushed as easily as a moth.
I heard a voice ask whether a mortal man can be more righteous than God.
I said God would save Job from six calamities, and even the seventh would not harm him.
I said Job's own mouth condemned him, and his own lips testified against him.
I said a man drinks in unrighteousness just like water.
I said gray-haired and aged men among Job's companions were much older than Job's father.
I said that then the Almighty would become Job's gold.
I told Job to throw his gold into the dust and the gold of Ophir into the rocky ravines.
I filled Job's hearing with a night vision, then later charged that there was no end to his errors.
I said God has no faith in his servants and finds fault with his angels.
I said even the heavens are not pure in God's eyes.
I spoke against Job three times before Jehovah said my anger-worthy words about Him were untrue.
I told Job that if he returned to the Almighty and removed unrighteousness from his tent, he would be restored.
I told Job to get to know God and he would be at peace.
Moses married my daughter.
I was a priest of Midian.
Zipporah was one of my daughters.
Moses cared for my flock before returning to Egypt.
Moses encountered the burning bush while leading my flock.
I had seven daughters.
My daughters told me about an Egyptian who rescued them from shepherds.
I welcomed Moses into my household after he fled from Egypt.
I asked my daughters where the man who helped them was and why they had left him behind.
I advised Moses to appoint capable men over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens.
I brought Moses' wife and sons to him in the wilderness.
I listened as Moses described Jehovah's deliverance of Israel from Egypt.
I offered sacrifices to God in the presence of Aaron and Israel's elders.
I watched Moses spend morning to evening serving as judge for the people.
I told Moses, "What you are doing is not good."
My advice helped establish a system of delegated judging in Israel.
I recommended choosing men who feared God, were trustworthy, and hated dishonest profit.
After visiting Israel's camp, Moses saw me off and I returned to my own land.
I lost my children, wealth, and health in a series of disasters.
I remained faithful despite severe suffering.
My body became covered with painful boils.
Satan claimed that I served God only because I was protected and prosperous.
Three companions came to comfort me during my suffering.
Before my trials I had seven sons and three daughters.
I lived in the land of Uz.
I regularly offered sacrifices on behalf of my children.
I said, "Jehovah gave, and Jehovah has taken away. Let the name of Jehovah continue to be praised."
I said, "Should we accept only what is good from the true God and not also accept what is bad?"
I was described as blameless, upright, and fearing God.
I was the greatest of all the Orientals.
My companions sat with me in silence for seven days and seven nights.
My wife urged me to curse God and die.
A younger man became angry with both me and my companions and later spoke at length.
Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar argued with me about my suffering.
Even if God killed me, I would wait for him and defend my ways before him.
I cursed the day of my birth.
I wished that my words could be written in a book and carved forever in rock.
I longed for an audience with God so that I could present my case.
I said I had been eyes to the blind and feet to the lame.
I said, "For I well know that my redeemer is alive."
I tore my garment, shaved my head, and fell to the ground when disaster struck.
I wished that I had died at birth.
In one day Sabeans, fire from the heavens, Chaldeans, and a great wind each brought me news of ruin.
After my trials, I received twice as much as I had before.
Afterward my brothers, sisters, and former acquaintances each gave me a piece of money and a gold ring.
I died old and satisfied with days.
I gave my daughters an inheritance among their brothers.
I lived for 140 years after my trials ended.
I made a covenant with my eyes.
I prayed in behalf of the very men who had criticized me.
I repented in dust and ashes after Jehovah answered me.
I said, "My ears have heard about you, but now I do see you with my eyes."
I said, "The thing I greatly feared has come upon me."
I scraped my skin with a piece of pottery while sitting among ashes.
I was questioned about Behemoth and Leviathan.
Jehovah asked me from a windstorm where I was when he founded the earth.
Jehovah told my companions to ask me to pray for them.
My daughters were named Jemimah, Keziah, and Keren-happuch.
My three daughters were more beautiful than all other women in the land.
I placed my baby in a papyrus basket among the reeds of the Nile.
I was paid to nurse my own son.
I was the mother of Moses.
I also bore Aaron and Miriam.
I belonged to the house of Levi.
I coated a papyrus basket with bitumen and pitch.
I was the wife of Amram.
When I saw how beautiful my son was, I kept him concealed.
After my son grew older, I brought him to the woman who had taken him from the Nile.
An Egyptian royal woman hired me to nurse the child I had hidden.
I was Amram's father's sister.
I was Levi's daughter, born to Levi in Egypt.
My daughter stood at a distance after I placed my son among the reeds.
When I could no longer conceal my son, I set him by the bank of the Nile.
By faith I hid my son for three months and did not fear the order of the king.
One of my sons became high priest, and the other led Israel out of Egypt.
I nursed the future deliverer of Israel while being paid by the woman who had drawn him from the water.
The child I hid in the Nile later became a son to the woman who found him.
I commanded Israel when Jericho fell.
I defeated Amalek and his people with the sword.
I led Israel across the Jordan into the Promised Land.
I said, "Sun, stand still over Gibeon, and moon, over the Valley of Aijalon!"
I succeeded Moses as leader of Israel.
I was one of the twelve spies sent into Canaan.
Only Caleb and I urged Israel to enter the Promised Land.
The sun stood still while I fought a battle.
From Shiloh I sent men to walk through the land and map it out.
I blessed Caleb and gave him Hebron as an inheritance.
I divided the Promised Land among the tribes of Israel.
I would not depart from the tent of meeting when Moses returned to the camp.
I said, "Do not fear the people of the land, for they are bread for us."
I urged the people not to rebel against Jehovah after the spies returned.
I was Moses' attendant while I was still a young man.
I was chosen to lead Israel after Moses was told he would not enter the Promised Land.
I was deceived by people who carried worn-out sandals and moldy bread.
I was of the tribe of Ephraim.
I went up from Gilgal to rescue Gibeon from five Amorite kings.
Descending with Moses, I said, “There is the sound of battle in the camp.”
I built an altar to Jehovah on Mount Ebal.
I gave God's command to priests carrying the Ark before Israel crossed the Jordan.
I made flint knives and circumcised the men of Israel at Gibeath-haaraloth.
I appointed twelve men to take twelve stones from the Jordan as a memorial.
I said, “Cursed be the man before Jehovah who undertakes to rebuild this city of Jericho.”
I sent two spies secretly into Jericho.
I was instructed to be courageous because Jehovah would be with me wherever I went.
Jehovah told Moses to write a memorial and repeat to me that He would wipe out the memory of Amalek.
Moses laid his hands on me before all Israel.
Rahab hid the men I sent to spy out a city.
When Eldad and Medad were prophesying, I said, “My lord Moses, restrain them!”
With Caleb I ripped my garments apart after the spies brought a bad report.
Hazor was the only city of that northern campaign that I burned.
I died at 110 years of age.
I fell facedown before Jehovah after Israel's defeat at Ai.
I hamstrung the horses of the northern kings and burned their chariots.
I marched around a fortified city for seven days before its walls collapsed.
I met a man with a drawn sword near Jericho.
I oversaw the judgment of the man who had taken devoted things from Jericho.
I renewed a covenant with Israel at Shechem.
I said, "As for me and my household, we will serve Jehovah."
I set up a large stone as a witness after speaking to the people.
I stretched out a javelin toward a city during battle.
I told my chiefs to place their feet on the backs of the necks of five kings taken from a cave at Makkedah.
I was told, "Remove your sandals from your feet, because the place where you are standing is holy."
Moses gave me a new name that I came to be known by.
The Israelites gave me Timnath-serah in the mountainous region of Ephraim, the city I asked for.
I rebelled against Moses and Aaron.
I died when fire consumed me along with 250 men.
I challenged the leadership that Jehovah had established for Israel.
I gathered 250 prominent men to support my rebellion.
I was a Kohathite Levite.
I argued that the entire congregation was holy.
I asked why Moses and Aaron had exalted themselves over the congregation.
Moses reminded me that I had already been given special service among the Levites.
I sought the priesthood in addition to my assigned responsibilities.
I stood at the entrance of the tent of meeting with censers.
The glory of Jehovah appeared while my rebellion was being judged.
Moses warned the people to move away from the tents associated with my rebellion.
I was a son of Izhar.
I was a descendant of Kohath.
I joined forces with Dathan and Abiram in a challenge to Moses.
Fire consumed the 250 men who offered incense in support of my rebellion.
The censers used in my rebellion were hammered into plating for the altar.
My rebellion became a warning against unauthorized priestly service.
A plague struck Israel after many people complained about the judgment connected to me.
Aaron stood between the dead and the living to stop a plague that followed my rebellion.
My name became associated with one of the most famous rebellions in Israel's wilderness history.
I belonged to the same broader Levitical family as Moses and Aaron.
I was not satisfied with the privileges I already had among God's people.
Later writers used my rebellion as an example of dangerous opposition to divine authority.
My sons survived even though I did not.
Some inspired songs were later associated with my descendants.
I was the sister of Moses and Aaron.
I watched over my baby brother after he was placed among the reeds of the Nile.
I suggested that Pharaoh's daughter hire my own mother to nurse my baby brother.
I was called a prophetess.
I led the women with tambourines after Israel crossed the Red Sea.
I sang, "Sing to Jehovah, for he has become highly exalted. The horse and its rider he has hurled into the sea."
I celebrated Jehovah's victory at the Red Sea with singing and dancing.
I took a tambourine in my hand, and many women followed me.
I spoke against Moses because of the Cushite woman he had married.
I questioned whether Jehovah had spoken only through Moses.
Jehovah defended my brother when I challenged his unique position.
I was struck with leprosy as white as snow.
Aaron pleaded with Moses after I was struck with leprosy.
Moses cried out, "O God, please heal her!" because of me.
I remained outside the camp for seven days.
The entire nation waited until I returned from quarantine before continuing its journey.
I died at Kadesh.
My death is recorded shortly before Israel's final approach to the Promised Land.
The prophet Micah later mentioned me alongside my two brothers.
God reminded Israel that he had sent Moses, Aaron, and I before them.
Jehovah asked why my brother and I did not fear to speak against His servant.
I led women in a victory song, but later I was disciplined after speaking against Moses.
My brother and I were not allowed to enter the Promised Land because we did not sanctify God before the eyes of the people.
I came down from the mountain carrying two stone tablets.
I died before Israel crossed the Jordan River.
I ground a golden calf into powder and made Israel drink it.
I removed my sandals because I was standing on holy ground.
I repeatedly went before Pharaoh with Jehovah's message.
I saw a thornbush that was on fire but was not being consumed.
I shattered the stone tablets when I saw Israel's idolatry.
I spent forty days and forty nights on Mount Sinai.
I stretched out my staff over the Red Sea.
I struck a rock instead of speaking to it.
I struck a rock so that water came out for the people.
I was adopted into Pharaoh's household.
I was born at a time when Hebrew baby boys were being put to death.
I was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians.
I was placed in an ark of papyrus among the reeds of the Nile.
I was told to lead the Israelites out of Egypt.
Jehovah buried me in the land of Moab.
Jehovah gave me the Ten Commandments.
Joshua succeeded me as Israel's leader.
My brother Aaron became my spokesman.
My face became radiant after speaking with Jehovah.
My mother hid me for three months after I was born.
My own mother was hired to nurse me.
No one knows my burial place to this day.
Pharaoh's daughter found me in the Nile.
I chose to be mistreated with God's people rather than enjoy the temporary pleasure of sin.
Aaron and Hur supported my hands until sunset.
I asked God what I should say if the Israelites wanted to know his name.
I asked one Hebrew, 'Why do you strike your companion?'
I said, 'Please show me your glory.'
I ate no bread and drank no water for forty days and forty nights on the mountain.
I became the father of Eliezer and Gershom.
I blessed the tribes of Israel before my death.
I carved out two stone tablets like the first ones I had shattered.
I gave Hoshea son of Nun the name Joshua.
I went up Mount Nebo and Jehovah showed me the Promised Land.
I commissioned Joshua by laying my hands on him.
I fled from Pharaoh to the land of Midian.
I hid the Egyptian's body in the sand.
I killed an Egyptian who was beating one of my fellow Hebrews.
I married Zipporah.
I pleaded with Jehovah not to destroy Israel after they made a golden calf.
I raised my hands during a battle, and Israel prevailed while they remained raised.
I realized my actions had become known after two Hebrews confronted me.
I went up and down Mount Sinai multiple times.
I rescued seven sisters from shepherds who were driving them away.
I returned to Egypt after hearing that those seeking my life were dead.
I said, "Pardon me, Jehovah, please send anyone whom you want to send."
I said, "Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh?"
I said, 'I have become a foreign resident in a foreign land.'
I said, 'If you are not going with us, do not lead us up from here.'
I spoke rashly before bringing water from a rock.
I threw my staff to the ground, and it became a serpent.
I told Jehovah that I was not a fluent speaker.
I took my position in the gate of the camp and said, “Who is on Jehovah's side? Come to me!”
I was eighty years old when I spoke to Pharaoh.
I was one hundred and twenty years old when I died.
I wrote a song to teach future generations.
Jehovah directed me to a tree, and when I threw it into the water at Marah, the water became sweet.
Jehovah spoke with me from the mountain while thunder and lightning surrounded it.
My father-in-law advised me to appoint capable men to help judge the people.
My hand became leprous and was then restored.
Water that I poured onto the ground became blood.
When my rod became a serpent, I fled from it.
By faith I kept the Passover and the sprinkling of the blood.
I appeared with Elijah during Jesus' transfiguration.
I asked Jehovah why he had allowed greater trouble to come upon His people.
I became a shepherd in Midian after living in Pharaoh's household.
I complained to Jehovah that the burden of leading the nation was too heavy for me.
I considered the reproach of the Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt.
I deposited twelve rods before Jehovah, and Aaron's rod budded, blossomed, and bore ripe almonds.
I heard Jehovah proclaim His own name and qualities before me.
I instructed Israel to observe the first Passover.
I lived with a priest of Midian.
I met Aaron at the mountain of the true God after Jehovah sent him to me.
I performed signs and miracles before Pharaoh and all Egypt.
I pleaded to pass over the Jordan and see the good land, but Jehovah said, “Enough from you!”
I prayed, 'O God, please heal her!'
I said, “If you are willing, pardon their sin; if not, please wipe me out from your book that you have written.”
I sent twelve men to spy out the Promised Land.
I spent about forty years in Midian before God called me.
I sprinkled blood on the people and said, “This is the blood of the covenant that Jehovah has made with you.”
I supervised the construction of the tabernacle according to the pattern shown to me.
I told the Israelites to apply blood to their doorposts.
I warned Pharaoh about the death of every firstborn in Egypt.
I wished that all of Jehovah's people were prophets.
I wrote this Law and had it placed beside the ark of the covenant of Jehovah.
Israel mourned me for thirty days.
Israel's elders believed after seeing the signs Jehovah had given me.
Jehovah described me as the most humble man on the face of the earth.
Jehovah placed me in a cleft of the rock while His glory passed by.
Jehovah sent quail after the people I led complained about the manna.
Jehovah showed me the entire Promised Land before my death.
Jehovah spoke with me face-to-face, as one man speaks to another.
Jesus said that I wrote about him.
My brother and sister spoke against me because of my Cushite wife.
My decision to help one Hebrew led to my exile from Egypt.
My eyesight had not grown dim, nor had my strength diminished when I died.
My father-in-law was also known as Reuel.
My first audience with Pharaoh resulted in harsher labor for the Israelites.
No prophet like me had yet arisen in Israel after my death.
On Mount Hor I removed Aaron's garments and clothed Eleazar his son with them.
At a lodging place, my wife circumcised our son with a flint.
Pharaoh sought to kill me after learning what I had done.
Seventy elders received some of the spirit that had been upon me.
The Devil disputed with Michael over my body.
The magicians of Egypt copied some of the early signs that Jehovah performed through me.
When I finished speaking with the Israelites, I would put a veil over my face.
When the Ark would set out, I said, “Rise up, Jehovah!”
With Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders of Israel, I saw a vision of the true God.
A bronze serpent was made during my leadership so that those who looked at it would live.
A pillar of cloud and a pillar of fire guided the nation I was leading.
A song bearing my name appears in both the Hebrew Scriptures and the Christian Greek Scriptures.
Balak wanted Balaam to curse the nation I was leading.
By faith I left Egypt, not fearing the rage of the king.
I announced that Jehovah would raise up a prophet like me, and Peter later applied that promise to Jesus.
I asked the Israelites to remember the day they left Egypt throughout future generations.
I carried Joseph's bones out of Egypt.
I faced Korah's rebellion during my leadership.
I instructed Aaron to take a censer into the congregation to stop a plague.
I interceded for Israel after they refused to enter the Promised Land.
I led Israel in singing after Jehovah's victory at the Red Sea.
I led Israel out of Egypt, but Joshua led them into the Promised Land.
I said, "Jehovah himself will fight for you, and you will keep silent."
I sang, "My strength and my might is Jah, since he has become my salvation."
I stretched out my hand again, and the sea returned upon the Egyptian army.
I stretched out my hand, and Jehovah drove the sea back with a strong east wind all night.
I told the frightened Israelites, "Do not be afraid. Stand firm and see the salvation of Jehovah."
I was faithful in all God's house as a servant.
Jehovah defended my leadership repeatedly when others challenged it.
Jehovah knew me 'face to face.'
Jehovah told me that my assistant would receive some of my authority.
Jesus compared his being lifted up to the copper serpent made in my day.
My brothers did not realize at first that God was using me to bring them salvation.
At forty I fled Egypt, and forty years later Jehovah appeared to me while I was tending a flock.
Paul used the veil I wore to explain the fading glory of the old covenant.
Paul wrote that our forefathers got baptized into me by means of the cloud and of the sea.
Stephen described me as being powerful in both my words and my deeds.
Stephen summarized my life as three periods of forty years each.
The Law covenant became closely associated with my name.
The man who rejected my intervention asked, 'Who appointed you ruler and judge over us?'
When I was forty years old, it came into my heart to see how my brothers, the sons of Israel, were doing.
Fire came out from before Jehovah and consumed me.
I offered unauthorized fire before Jehovah.
I was Aaron's firstborn.
I was a son of Aaron.
I died before Jehovah in the wilderness of Sinai.
I saw a vision of the true God.
I was named among Aaron's sons summoned to serve as priests.
I went up with Moses, Aaron, my brother, and 70 elders of Israel.
My brother and I each took a fire holder and placed incense on it.
My mother was Elisheba.
After I died, Eleazar and Ithamar continued to serve as priests with Aaron.
After seeing a vision of the true God, I ate and drank.
I did not have any sons.
I was an anointed priest who had been installed to serve.
Jehovah had not commanded the fire I offered.
Jehovah told Moses to bring me up before the covenant was confirmed.
My cousins carried me outside the camp in my robes.
A later census still recorded that I died for presenting unauthorized fire before Jehovah.
After seeing a vision of the true God, I later offered fire He had not commanded.
I died after fire from Jehovah had just consumed the inaugural offerings on the altar.
Moses told Aaron that Jehovah would be made holy among those near to him after I died.
Under God's feet I saw what seemed like a sapphire pavement.
I came out to fight Israel at Edrei.
I was king of Bashan.
Israel defeated me and took possession of my land.
I went out against Israel with all my people.
Rahab later said she had heard what Jehovah did to Sihon and to me.
Jehovah told Moses not to be afraid of me.
I was one of the last of the Rephaim.
I reigned in Ashtaroth and Edrei.
Israel struck me down along with my sons and all my people, until none survived.
My cities were fortified with high walls, gates, and bars.
My kingdom included 60 cities in the region of Argob.
A psalm later named me among the mighty kings Jehovah struck down.
My iron bier was nine cubits long and four cubits wide, and it was kept in Rabbah of the Ammonites.
I helped do the work of the holy service for the tabernacle.
I was filled with skill for sacred craftsmanship.
Jehovah appointed me to assist Bezalel.
I belonged to the tribe of Dan.
Jehovah put it into my heart to teach, along with Bezalel.
Moses called Bezalel and me to the construction work.
I was the son of Ahisamach.
I worked with blue thread, purple wool, scarlet material, and fine linen.
Jehovah appointed me so that skillful workers could make everything he had commanded Moses.
Bezalel was called from Judah, and I was appointed from Dan to assist him.
I was skilled for the work of a craftsman, an embroiderer, a weaver, and a loom worker.
The record names me with Bezalel when summarizing who carried out the holy work.
I enslaved the Israelites.
I ordered the death of every newborn Hebrew boy.
I ordered the Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah to put newborn Israelite boys to death.
I was a new king who did not know Joseph.
I asked, "Who is Jehovah, that I should obey his voice...?"
Moses repeatedly appeared before me with Jehovah's message.
My forces were overwhelmed in the Red Sea.
I repeatedly hardened my heart.
I stopped supplying straw but still demanded the same number of bricks.
I suggested that only the men should leave to worship Jehovah.
I summoned Moses and Aaron many times during a series of devastating plagues.
Jehovah also allowed my heart to become obstinate in order to display His power.
After letting Israel leave, I changed my mind and pursued them.
I admitted, "I have sinned this time. Jehovah is righteous."
I asked Moses to plead with Jehovah to remove several of the plagues.
I confessed my sin again after the plague of locusts.
I finally released the Israelites after the death of the firstborn.
I offered to let Israel sacrifice inside the land instead of leaving.
I suggested that Israel leave their livestock behind.
I threatened to kill Moses if he appeared before me again.
I took six hundred chosen chariots with me when pursuing Israel.
My magic-practicing priests said, “It is the finger of God!”
A later inspired writer used me as an example of someone who stubbornly opposed God's purpose.
At night I called Moses and Aaron and told them to get out from among my people.
During the darkness my people could not see one another, but the Israelites had light where they lived.
Jehovah said He had allowed me to continue existing in order to declare His name throughout the earth.
My own firstborn died during the final plague.
My refusal to submit resulted in Egypt experiencing ten devastating plagues.
I drew a Hebrew baby out of the water and named him Moses.
I found a crying baby in a basket among the reeds.
I took a Hebrew child and brought him up as my own son.
I felt compassion for the crying boy.
I hired a Hebrew woman to nurse the child for me.
I paid the child's own mother to nurse him.
I said, “This is one of the children of the Hebrews.”
I sent my slave girl to get a basket from among the reeds.
I went down to bathe in the Nile while my female attendants walked by the side of the river.
I opened the basket myself and saw the child inside.
I said, “It is because I have drawn him out of the water.”
When a Hebrew girl offered to call a nursing woman, I told her to go.
When the child grew older, he was brought to me and became a son to me.
I preserved a Hebrew child my father the king had ordered put to death.
I unknowingly paid a Hebrew mother to nurse the very child she had hidden on the Nile.
The boy I raised later refused to be called my son.
The son I brought up was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians.
I followed the Israelite and Midianite woman into the tent and pierced them both with a spear.
I saw an Israelite take a Midianite woman into his tent during a plague.
I was a grandson of Aaron.
I was a son of Eleazar.
I went to war against Midian carrying the holy utensils and the trumpets for signaling.
My action stopped a plague among the Israelites.
The Israelite man I pierced was a chieftain of a Simeonite paternal house.
The Midianite woman I pierced was the daughter of a Midianite chieftain.
A psalm later said that what I did was counted to me as righteousness for generation after generation forever.
During a civil conflict involving Benjamin, I was serving before the ark and inquired of God.
I went with ten chiefs to investigate an altar built by the tribes east of the Jordan.
I approved the explanation given by the tribes east of the Jordan regarding a disputed altar.
Jehovah gave me a covenant of peace and a lasting priesthood.
Jehovah said that I turned His wrath away from the Israelites because I tolerated no rivalry toward Him.
I kept Hebrew baby boys alive.
I would not do what the king of Egypt told me.
The king of Egypt spoke to me about Hebrew childbirth.
I reported that Hebrew women were lively and gave birth quickly.
The king of Egypt told me and my fellow midwife how to act when we saw a Hebrew woman on the stool for childbirth.
Shiphrah served with me among the Hebrew midwives.
I answered the king of Egypt after he learned that Hebrew boys were being kept alive.
My fear of the true God was followed by God giving me a family.
The king of Egypt summoned me and demanded to know why the male children were still alive.
My defiance as a midwife came before the king's wider Nile decree against every Hebrew newborn son.
The king of Egypt first tried to stop Israel through me and my coworker, then through all his people.
When answering the king of Egypt, I contrasted Hebrew mothers with Egyptian women.
I hid two Israelite spies.
I lived in Jericho.
I tied a scarlet cord in my window.
Joshua instructed that my household be spared when Jericho was destroyed.
A scarlet cord in my window became the sign by which my household would be identified.
My house was built into the city wall.
I was told to gather my family inside my house for their safety.
The king of Jericho sent messengers looking for the men who had come to my house.
I came to live among the Israelites after the fall of Jericho.
I believed that Jehovah had given the land to Israel before my city fell.
I said that the fear of Israel had fallen upon my people.
I declared, "Jehovah your God is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath."
I said, "I had heard what Jehovah did to the Red Sea and to Sihon and Og."
I hid two men beneath stalks of flax on my roof.
I became an ancestress of King David.
Two Israelite men stayed hidden in the hill country for three days after leaving my house.
A later Bible writer cited my works as evidence that faith must be accompanied by action.
My faith preserved not only my life but also the lives of my family.
I misdirected my king's messengers to protect two foreigners.
I asked that my family receive the same loyal love I showed to two strangers.
The agreement of protection made with me did not cover anyone leaving my house.
I feared the true God and kept the male children alive.
I was a Hebrew midwife in Egypt.
The king of Egypt ordered me to put newborn Hebrew boys to death.
I explained that Hebrew women had already given birth before a midwife could come in to them.
Puah worked with me as a midwife.
The king of Egypt told me that if the newborn was a daughter, she must live.
Because I feared the true God, he later gave me a family.
God dealt well with me after I refused the king's command.
The king of Egypt called me in and asked why the male children had been kept alive.
God dealt well with me at the same time Israel kept increasing and becoming very mighty.
I told the king of Egypt that Hebrew women were not like Egyptian women.
The king of Egypt had already failed to make me kill Hebrew sons before he ordered all his people to throw them into the Nile.
I refused to let Israel pass through my territory.
I was a king of the Amorites.
I was king of Heshbon.
Heshbon was my city.
I went out against Israel in battle at Jahaz.
Israel asked to march through my land on the King's Road.
Before Israel came, I had fought Moab and taken land as far as the Arnon.
Israel took my land from the Arnon to the Jabbok.
Jehovah allowed my spirit to become obstinate and my heart to become hard.
Moses sent me peaceful messengers from the wilderness of Kedemoth.
After my defeat, a taunting proverb was composed about my city.
Jephthah later recounted that I would not trust Israel to cross my land and that I fought at Jahaz.
Later songs remembered me as a mighty Amorite king Jehovah struck down.
I had no sons.
I was the father of five daughters.
My daughters appealed to Moses because I left no sons.
Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah were my daughters.
I belonged to the tribe of Manasseh.
I died in the wilderness.
My daughters received an inheritance in my name.
Jehovah ruled in favor of my daughters' request.
I died for my own sin, not because I joined Korah's rebellion.
My name was preserved through my daughters instead of through sons.
My daughters stood before Moses, Eleazar, the chieftains, and the entire assembly.
My family's case became the basis for Israel's inheritance law when a man died without a son.
My daughters obeyed the instruction to marry within our father's tribal family.
My inheritance was granted after my death because my daughters spoke up.
Joshua later carried out Jehovah's command concerning my family's inheritance.
I was the wife of Moses.
I was the daughter of Jethro.
I was a Midianite.
I had two sons with Moses.
My sons were named Gershom and Eliezer.
I met Moses after he fled from Egypt.
My father gave me to Moses as his wife.
I circumcised my son with a flint.
After Moses had sent me away, I was reunited with him in the wilderness.
My father brought me and my two sons back to Moses.
I spoke of a 'bridegroom of blood' after circumcising my son.
My husband named one of our sons because he had become a foreign resident.
One of my sons was named to express that Jehovah had helped Moses against Pharaoh.
I was reunited with Moses after Israel had already left Egypt.
My father witnessed Moses recount Jehovah's deliverance after bringing me back to him.
Along with Job's other two companions, I spent seven days and seven nights sitting on the ground with him in silence.
Along with Job's other two companions, I threw dust into the air and onto my head when I saw him from far off.
I answered Job during the long debate over his suffering.
I came with Job's other two companions to sympathize with him.
Jehovah said that Job's three companions, including me, had not spoken the truth about Him as Job had.
Job prayed for his three companions, including me, and Jehovah accepted that prayer.
Along with Job's other two companions, I offered the burnt sacrifice Jehovah required.
I came with Eliphaz and Bildad after agreeing to meet together.
I said God knows when men are deceitful and takes notice of what is evil.
I said Job's life would become brighter than midday.
I said that if Job put wrongdoing far away, he could lift up his face with no defect.
I told Job to prepare his heart and stretch out his hands to God.
I was a Naamathite.
I wished that God would speak and open his lips to Job.
After only two speeches, I stopped answering Job along with his other two companions.
I asked whether Job could discover the deep things of God, or everything about the Almighty.
I said God allows some of a person's error to be forgotten.
I said God's wisdom is higher than heaven and deeper than the Grave.
I said I had heard a reproof that insulted me, so my understanding impelled me to reply.
I said an empty-headed man will understand only when a wild donkey can give birth to a man.
I said the joyful cry of the wicked is brief, and the rejoicing of the godless is for a moment.
I said the wicked man swallows wealth but will vomit it up.
I said the wicked will never see streams of water, the torrents of honey and butter.
I said the wicked will suck the venom of cobras, and the fangs of a viper will kill him.
My own troubling thoughts urged me to answer Job because of the agitation I felt.
I said a fire that no one fanned will consume the wicked man.
I said heaven will uncover the wicked man's error, and the earth will rise up against him.
I said the wicked man will perish forever like his own dung.
I told Job that practical wisdom has many sides, then later answered him from agitation and insult.
